analysis.one_liner: Suspends faster slaughterhouse line-speed waivers during the COVID emergency to protect meat and poultry workers.
analysis.headline: The bill to freeze faster meat-plant line speeds during the COVID emergency died in committee with 34 cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, meat and poultry plants were allowed to run slaughter lines faster under waivers from the Department of Agriculture. This bill would have suspended those waivers and stopped any new ones, frozen the new swine slaughter inspection system, and required USDA, Labor, and Health and Human Services to report on what they did to protect workers, animals, and food safety. The Department would also have been barred from spending money on any program that increases line speeds during the emergency.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry plant workers, whose jobs require them to stand shoulder to shoulder on fast-moving lines; food safety inspectors, who would see inspection staffing rules protected; consumers, who would get a slower, more inspected supply of meat during the pandemic; and the public, through a mandated government review of how agencies protected workers and food during COVID.

how_it_helps.text: The bill suspends all existing line-speed waivers and blocks new ones at covered meat and poultry establishments for the duration of the COVID-19 emergency, plus 90 days.
It suspends implementation of and conversion to the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System, the 2019 rule that let pork plants run at unlimited line speeds.
It prohibits any USDA funds from being used to develop or implement any program that would increase line speeds at these plants during the emergency period.

It requires the Secretaries of Agriculture, Labor, and Health and Human Services to report to Congress by December 31, 2020 on what they did to protect workers and food safety, and requires a Government Accountability Office review of those actions after the emergency ends.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing companies, which could not raise line speeds during the emergency and would keep slower lines while inspection staffing rules were protected, cutting output per hour.

drawbacks.text: The freeze applies only during the COVID-19 emergency period plus 90 days, so the underlying line-speed rules would come back unchanged afterward.

Processors and some food-supply officials argued that slower lines reduce processing capacity, a concern during a pandemic when plant closures already disrupted the meat supply; the bill does not provide any offsetting capacity relief.
The bill addresses line speeds and inspection staffing but does not itself provide workers with paid sick leave, hazard pay, or enforcement of physical distancing beyond the reporting requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, temporary freeze rather than a permanent fix: it buys slower lines and protected inspection staffing during the pandemic and forces agencies to account for their record, but it expires with the emergency and does not tackle wages, sick leave, or the underlying pace-of-work rules. The cost falls on processing companies' output during a period when they were profiting from federal contracts; the benefit is reduced risk of injury and infection for one of the pandemic's most exposed workforces.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee from July 2020 until the Congress ended, sent to a subcommittee but never marked up or brought to the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcia Fudge introduced the Safe Line Speeds in COVID-19 Act on July 9, 2020, with Reps. DeLauro and Thompson of Mississippi as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Agriculture, Education and Labor, and Energy and Commerce Committees on the day of introduction.
On September 11, 2020 it was referred to the Agriculture Committee's Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture, where no further action was taken.
The bill had 34 cosponsors, 33 Democrats and 1 Republican, but never received a markup or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
No vote was ever held, so the line-speed waivers and the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System stayed in place, and the required agency reports and GAO review were never mandated.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processing companies kept their faster line speeds and the swine inspection system throughout the pandemic emergency, and no GAO review of worker and food safety was required. Plant workers, who faced some of the country's worst COVID outbreaks, got no federal line-speed relief.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 34 cosponsors, 33 were Democrats and 1 was a Republican; it never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Faster line speeds raise output and profit per hour, and USDA waivers plus the 2019 swine inspection rule allowed plants to run lines faster with fewer federal inspectors; the bill would suspend those waivers and freeze any further speed increases for the duration of the emergency. Slower lines mean lower throughput for the industry, which is why its interest in this bill ran against the workers whose safety the bill was protecting.

industries.industry: Federal meat and poultry inspection workforce
industries.note: The bill suspends line-speed waivers together with changes to inspection staffing requirements, preserving federal inspector coverage while plants would otherwise speed up, and requires agencies to report on inspector protections during COVID.
